# Why isn't my ac working after I jumped the car?

Jump-starting a vehicle involves connecting external power to a depleted battery, but it introduces significant electrical transients that can trigger protective mechanisms in sensitive electronic control modules. In your case, involving a 1999 Saturn SC2, the lack of AC functionality immediately following this procedure suggests that the system has entered a fault state or lost its calibration data. When you press the AC button and see the green indicator illuminate, but feel no additional drag on the serpentine belt (the compressor clutch), and observe no change in airflow when engaging recirculation, the vehicle's Body Control Module (BCM) or Climate Control Module is likely ignoring requests from the user interface.

The absence of a "drag" sensation on the engine or steering wheel is a primary diagnostic clue. The AC compressor is typically engaged by an electromagnetic clutch located on the front pulley. When the system activates, this clutch pulls down to engage the belt; without power reaching the clutch coil or the control signal telling it to engage, the belt remains unloaded. Since you are seeing the green light, the dashboard switch logic is functioning, but the downstream actuation is failing. This disconnect points toward either a blown fuse, a tripped relay, or a communication error between the BCM and the A/C compressor clutch driver.

Jump-starts can introduce voltage spikes that exceed the nominal 12V supply. Modern automotive ECUs often have capacitors to absorb these surges, but repeated or high-energy spikes can damage internal regulators or corrupt non-volatile memory if not properly managed. In older vehicles like your Saturn SC2, which predates some of the more robust fault isolation found in newer models, a voltage spike might have caused the BCM to latch into a "safe mode." In this state, the module disables high-load accessories like the AC compressor to prevent overheating or further electrical damage, even though it allows low-power functions like dashboard illumination to remain active.

Before assuming a mechanical failure of the compressor itself, you should verify the power distribution path. The most common point of failure after an electrical disturbance is the main fuse for the A/C system. Check the under-hood fuse box and the interior fuse panel for the specific fuse labeled "A/C" or "Climate Control." If this fuse has blown due to a transient short, it will need replacement. However, if you replace the fuse and it blows again immediately, there is likely a shorted component downstream, such as the compressor clutch coil or a wiring harness issue.

Another potential culprit is the relays controlling the AC system. The relay that powers the compressor clutch may have welded contacts open due to heat or the voltage spike, preventing current from flowing even though the control signal is present. You can test this by swapping the A/C relay with an identical relay from another circuit, such as the fuel pump relay (if applicable) or the horn relay, provided they share the same pinout and amperage rating.

It is also possible that the system requires a reset sequence. Some GM vehicles of this era may need the ignition cycled off and on multiple times to clear a temporary fault code stored in the BCM's memory. If the module has logged a "High Side" or "Low Side" pressure sensor fault, it will disable the compressor until the issue is resolved. Unfortunately, without a scan tool capable of reading GM-specific trouble codes (P-codes) for the HVAC system, diagnosing internal sensor failures can be difficult.

If the fuse checks out and swapping relays yields no result, the issue may lie within the BCM itself. The module might have suffered a latch-up event where its internal logic is stuck in a disabled state for that specific output line. At this point, replacing the BCM or seeking professional diagnosis with a bi-directional scan tool to command the clutch directly is often necessary. The cost of parts like the compressor or the ECM should be weighed against the likelihood of simple fuse or relay issues first.
